title: Cybersecurity Examples
description: Small Cybersecurity Fundamentals examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Protect information
examples.description: Security includes keeping information private, correct and available when needed. These three goals are often called confidentiality, integrity and availability.
examples.code:
Private: only the teacher sees a private note
Correct: a score is not changed by accident
Available: the lesson page opens when needed

examples.title: Think about the thing you protect
examples.description: An asset is something valuable, such as a file or saved work. A threat is something that might harm it. A risk considers how likely and harmful that problem is.
examples.code:
Asset: a class project file
Threat: accidental deletion
Control: a tested backup copy

examples.title: Use strong unique passwords
examples.description: A unique password is used for only one account. A password manager can create and remember long passwords so one leak does not unlock many accounts.
examples.code:
Account A: its own long password
Account B: a different long password
Password manager: stores them in its protected vault

examples.title: Add another sign-in factor
examples.description: Multi-factor authentication asks for more than one kind of proof. A security key or an authenticator can add protection beyond a password.
examples.code:
Something you know: password
Something you have: security key
Two factors protect one sign-in

examples.title: Spot suspicious messages
examples.description: Phishing is a trick that tries to make someone reveal information or take a harmful action. Pause when a message pressures you to act quickly.
examples.code:
Message: Your school files vanish in 5 minutes! Send your password now.
Safer response: do not reply; contact the school through a known channel.

examples.title: Check the actual address
examples.description: A link label can differ from its destination. Read the real host name carefully before entering private information.
examples.code:
Label shown: School portal
Actual host: school.example.attacker.test
Domain controlled here: attacker.test

examples.title: Keep software updated
examples.description: Updates often fix known weaknesses as well as ordinary bugs. Install them through the software's trusted update route.
examples.code:
Known issue discovered
Maker publishes a fix
You update and restart when required

examples.title: Give only needed access
examples.description: Least privilege means giving each person or program only the access needed for its job. This limits damage from mistakes or misuse.
examples.code:
Reader: can view lesson files
Editor: can change lesson text
Publisher: can release a reviewed version

examples.title: Treat text as text
examples.description: User-supplied text should not become executable page code by accident. textContent places text into a page without treating it as HTML.

examples.title: Validate at a trusted boundary
examples.description: Validation checks that data follows a rule. Browser checks help the user, but a real backend must check received data too because browser code can be changed.
examples.code:
Page rule: quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 5
Backend rule in a real service: check the same limits before saving
This tutorial app: has no backend or accounts

examples.title: Back up and practise recovery
examples.description: A backup is another copy of important data. A useful backup must be readable and restorable, not merely present.
examples.code:
Working file: project.txt
Backup copy: stored separately
Recovery practice: open a copy and check the contents

examples.title: Respond calmly to a problem
examples.description: An incident is an event that may harm security. Stop risky actions, preserve useful facts and get help from the responsible person.
examples.code:
Unexpected sign-in notice
1. Do not follow the message link
2. Open the service through a known address
3. Review activity and contact its support if needed
